subject: cs
book: Computer Science Textbook for Class XII (NCERT)

sections.name: Revision of Class XI Python (CBSE syllabus)

concepts.text: Python basics recap: tokens, keywords, identifiers, literals, variables, comments, input() and print()
Data types recap: int, float, complex, bool, str, list, tuple, dict, None; mutable versus immutable types
Operators and precedence recap: arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment/augmented, identity, membership
Type conversion recap: implicit and explicit conversion
Control statements recap: if-elif-else, for with range(), while, break, continue, nested loops
Strings, lists, tuples and dictionaries recap: indexing, slicing, common methods and built-in functions
Exercise types: predict output, find and correct errors, evaluate expressions, write short programs

sections.name: 7.1-7.2 Introduction to Functions (NCERT Class XI Functions chapter)

concepts.text: Function as a named block of code that performs a specific task
Advantages of functions: modularity, reusability, readability, easier testing and teamwork
Types of functions: built-in functions, functions defined in modules, user-defined functions
Defining a function with def, function header, parameters, colon and indented body
Calling (invoking) a function; a function must be defined before it is called
Docstrings and function naming
Parameter (in definition) versus argument (value passed in the call)
Positional arguments: values matched to parameters by order
Default parameters: parameters with default values must come after non-default ones
Keyword (named) arguments in calls
Passing strings, lists and other objects as arguments; effect of mutable arguments
return statement; functions with and without return (void functions return None)
Returning multiple values as a tuple and unpacking them
Function types by arguments and return: with/without arguments, with/without return value
Order in which statements run when functions are defined and called; tracing flow with line numbers
Local variables: defined inside a function, accessible only there
Global variables: defined outside functions, accessible throughout the program
Using the global keyword to modify a global variable inside a function
Name resolution when local and global names clash (local shadows global)
Commonly used built-ins: input(), print(), int(), float(), str(), len(), type(), abs(), divmod(), max(), min(), pow(), sum(), round(), range()
Using modules: import and from-import (math, random, statistics) as library functions
Creating and importing a user-defined module
Programs: functions for factorial, prime check, calculator, area of shapes, list statistics, string processing
Exercise types: trace output of function code, identify local/global, write functions with default and positional parameters
Errors can stop a program, give wrong output or cause abnormal behaviour
Exceptions can be raised automatically by Python or deliberately by the programmer, and can be handled
Syntax (parsing) errors occur when language rules are broken; program won't run until fixed
How syntax errors are reported in shell mode versus script mode
Exception as an error during execution (e.g. missing file, division by zero) that disrupts normal flow
An exception is a Python object; unhandled exceptions terminate the program
SyntaxError, IndentationError
ValueError (right type, wrong value) and TypeError (wrong type in an operation)
ZeroDivisionError, OverflowError
IndexError (index out of range), NameError (undefined name), KeyError (missing dictionary key)
IOError (file cannot be opened), EOFError (end of file on input), ImportError (module not found), KeyboardInterrupt (user interrupts)
Programmer-raised exceptions to signal errors
raise statement: raise ExceptionName('message')
assert statement: assert condition, message; raises AssertionError when false
Need for exception handling: separate main logic from error-handling code, prevent crashes
Process: exception object created, thrown, runtime searches the call stack for a handler, handler catches it
Catching exceptions with try and except blocks
Multiple except clauses for different exceptions and a generic except
try...except...else: else runs when no exception occurs
finally block always runs whether or not an exception occurred
Using finally for cleanup such as closing files; recovering and continuing after an exception
Exercise types: identify exception raised by given code, write try-except-else-finally programs, predict output, use raise/assert
Need for files: data in variables is lost when the program ends; files store data permanently
File as a named location on secondary storage
Text files: human-readable characters, lines ending with EOL (\n), encoded as ASCII/Unicode
Binary files: bytes not readable as text (images, audio, pickled objects)
CSV files as text files with comma-separated values (CBSE syllabus)
Relative and absolute paths to a file (CBSE syllabus)

sections.name: 2.3 Opening and Closing a Text File

concepts.text: open(file_name, access_mode) returns a file object; file object attributes name, mode, closed
Text file modes r, r+, w, w+, a, a+ and where the file pointer starts in each
Closing a file with close() and why it matters (flushing the buffer)
Opening a file using the with clause (auto-close)
write(string) writes a string and returns the number of characters written; converting numbers with str()
writelines(list_of_strings) writes several strings at once
Appending data in a/a+ mode versus overwriting in w mode
read([n]) reads n characters or the whole file
readline([n]) reads one line at a time
readlines() returns a list of all lines; using split() and loops to process lines and words
tell() returns the current position of the file pointer
seek(offset, reference_point) moves the file pointer (0 beginning, 1 current, 2 end)

sections.name: 2.7 Creating and Traversing a Text File

concepts.text: Creating a file and writing data entered by the user
Traversing a file and displaying data line by line
Performing read and write on the same file (r+/w+)
Manipulating text file data: count lines, words, characters, vowels; display lines starting with a letter; copy selected lines to another file
Serialization (pickling) and de-serialization (unpickling) of Python objects
Binary file modes rb, rb+, wb, wb+, ab, ab+
pickle.dump(object, file) to write and pickle.load(file) to read; EOFError at end of file
Binary file operations: create/write, read all records, search for a record, append records, update a record
Importing the csv module; opening/closing CSV files and the newline='' argument
Writing with csv.writer(), writerow() and writerows()
Reading with csv.reader() and iterating over rows
Programs: store and search student/employee records in a CSV file
Exercise types: differentiate text/binary files and modes, write file-processing functions, predict output of seek/tell
Data structure as a way to store and organise data for efficient use; linear data structures
Stack as a LIFO (Last In First Out) linear structure with insertion and deletion at one end (top)
Real-life examples: pile of plates, stack of books
Applications: reversing a string, undo/redo in editors, browser back button, matching parentheses
PUSH: add an element at the top; overflow when a fixed-size stack is full
POP: remove the top element; underflow when the stack is empty
Other operations: peek/top, isEmpty, size, display
Using a Python list as a stack: append() for push and pop() for pop
Writing functions isEmpty(), opPush(), opPop(), top(), size() and display() for a stack
Menu-driven stack program; push/pop of records (e.g. lists or dictionaries meeting a condition) as in board questions

sections.name: 3.5 Notations for Arithmetic Expressions (in NCERT book; beyond CBSE 083 exam syllabus)

concepts.text: Infix, prefix (Polish) and postfix (reverse Polish) notations

sections.name: 3.6 Conversion from Infix to Postfix Notation (in NCERT book; beyond CBSE 083 exam syllabus)

concepts.text: Stack-based algorithm for converting an infix expression to postfix using operator precedence and parentheses

sections.name: 3.7 Evaluation of Postfix Expression (in NCERT book; beyond CBSE 083 exam syllabus)

concepts.text: Evaluating a postfix expression with a stack, step by step
Exercise types: trace stack contents after push/pop sequences, write push/pop functions, reverse a string using a stack
Computer network as interconnected devices (nodes/hosts) sharing data and resources
Benefits of networking: resource sharing, communication, data sharing
ARPANET (1969) as the first network
NSFNET and the growth into the Internet; key milestones (TCP/IP, email, WWW)
PAN (Personal Area Network): around a person, a few metres
LAN (Local Area Network): within a building or campus
MAN (Metropolitan Area Network): across a city
WAN (Wide Area Network): across countries; the Internet as the largest WAN
Modem: modulation/demodulation between digital and analog signals
Ethernet card (NIC) and RJ45 connector; Wi-Fi card
Repeater: regenerates weak signals
Hub: broadcasts data to all ports
Switch: forwards data only to the intended device
Router: connects networks and routes packets
Gateway: connects networks using different protocols; access point
Mesh topology: every node connected to every other
Ring topology: nodes in a closed loop
Bus topology: all nodes on a single backbone cable
Star topology: nodes connected to a central hub/switch
Tree (hierarchical) topology: combination of star and bus
Advantages and disadvantages of each topology; choosing a topology/layout for a given case

sections.name: 10.6 Identifying Nodes in a Networked Communication

concepts.text: MAC address: unique 48-bit physical address of a NIC
IP address: logical address; IPv4 (32-bit) and IPv6 (128-bit)

sections.name: 10.7 Internet, Web and the Internet of Things

concepts.text: Internet versus World Wide Web
Internet of Things (IoT): everyday devices connected to the internet
Domain names and their parts (top-level domains like .com, .in)
DNS servers and name resolution (domain name to IP address)
WWW, HTML (presentation of web pages) and XML (data with user-defined tags), HTML versus XML
URL and its parts; website and web page
Web browser and web server
Web hosting
Exercise types: case-study network design (layout, device placement, best connection), differences (hub vs switch, LAN vs WAN), match device to function
Data communication as exchange of data between devices over a medium
Sender, receiver, message, communication media and protocols
Bandwidth as the range of frequencies a channel can carry (Hz, kHz, MHz, GHz)
Data transfer rate in bits per second (bps, Kbps, Mbps, Gbps) and unit conversions
Simplex (one way, e.g. keyboard to computer)
Half-duplex (both ways, one at a time, e.g. walkie-talkie)
Full-duplex (both ways simultaneously, e.g. telephone)
Circuit switching: dedicated path set up before communication (telephone)
Packet switching: data split into packets that travel independently and are reassembled
Comparison of circuit and packet switching
Guided (wired) versus unguided (wireless) media
Twisted pair cable (UTP/STP): features, advantages, limitations
Coaxial cable: features, advantages, limitations
Optical fibre: light signals, high bandwidth, immune to interference, costly
Radio waves: omnidirectional, penetrate walls (e.g. Wi-Fi, FM radio)
Microwaves: line-of-sight, unidirectional (e.g. satellite, cellular links)
Infrared waves: very short range, cannot pass walls (e.g. remote controls)
Wireless technologies: Bluetooth and Wireless LAN
Generations 1G (analog voice), 2G (digital, SMS), 3G (mobile internet), 4G (high-speed data), 5G (very high speed, low latency)
Need for protocols: rules for format, timing and error control in communication
HTTP for web pages and HTTPS as its secure version
FTP for file transfer
PPP for direct point-to-point links
SMTP for sending email and POP3 for receiving email
TCP/IP for reliable packet delivery and addressing
TELNET for remote login and VoIP for voice calls over the internet (CBSE syllabus)
Exercise types: identify communication type, choose transmission medium for a case, protocol for a task, convert data-rate units
Need to store and manage large amounts of data in an organised way (e.g. student attendance records)
Storing data in files and its limitations
Difficulty in access and data redundancy (duplicate data)
Data inconsistency, data isolation and data dependence
Controlled data sharing is difficult in a file system
Database and DBMS: software to create, store, manage and retrieve data (e.g. MySQL, Oracle)
Real-life applications of DBMS: banking, railway reservation, library, school records
Key concepts: database schema, data constraints, meta-data (data dictionary), database instance
Key concepts: query, data manipulation (insert, update, delete) and database engine
Relation (table) made of rows and columns
Attribute (column), tuple (row), domain (allowed values of an attribute)
Degree (number of attributes) and cardinality (number of tuples); computing them for given tables
Properties of a relation: unique attribute names, distinct tuples, atomic values, order of rows/columns does not matter
Meaning of NULL value
Candidate key: attribute(s) that can uniquely identify a tuple
Primary key: candidate key chosen to identify tuples; cannot be NULL
Alternate key: candidate keys not chosen as primary key (CBSE syllabus)
Composite primary key: primary key made of two or more attributes
Foreign key: attribute referring to the primary key of another relation; referential integrity
Exercise types: identify keys, degree and cardinality in given tables; file system vs DBMS differences
RDBMS software examples: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL
SQL as a declarative, case-insensitive query language; statements end with semicolon
Categories of SQL commands: DDL (Data Definition Language) and DML (Data Manipulation Language)

sections.name: 9.3 Data Types and Constraints in MySQL

concepts.text: Data types: CHAR(n) (fixed length) versus VARCHAR(n) (variable length), INT, FLOAT, DATE
Constraints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY
CREATE DATABASE, SHOW DATABASES, USE database, DROP DATABASE
CREATE TABLE with data types and constraints; SHOW TABLES
DESCRIBE (DESC) table to view structure
ALTER TABLE: add/remove an attribute, add/remove primary key, add foreign key, modify column
DROP TABLE; DROP versus DELETE
INSERT INTO to add records, with and without a column list
Order of insertion when foreign keys exist
UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE to modify records; ALTER versus UPDATE
DELETE FROM ... WHERE to remove records
SELECT statement to retrieve all columns (*) or selected columns
Column aliasing with AS and computed columns
DISTINCT clause to remove duplicates
WHERE clause with relational, logical (AND, OR, NOT) and mathematical operators
BETWEEN for ranges and IN / NOT IN for membership
ORDER BY in ascending and descending order
Handling NULL with IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
Pattern matching with LIKE using % and _ wildcards
Single-row functions versus aggregate (multi-row) functions
Aggregate functions: MAX(), MIN(), AVG(), SUM(), COUNT() and COUNT(*), and how they treat NULL
GROUP BY to group rows and apply aggregate functions per group
HAVING clause to filter groups; WHERE versus HAVING
Cartesian product of two relations: degree and cardinality of the result

sections.name: 9.10 Using Two Relations in a Query

concepts.text: Cartesian product on two tables in a SELECT query
Equi-join: joining tables on equality of a common attribute using WHERE or JOIN ... ON
Natural join: join on common attribute, showing it once
Table aliases when querying two tables
Exercise types: write queries on given tables, predict query output, create database/tables with constraints, differentiate commands

chapters.title: Interface of Python with an SQL Database

sections.name: Connecting SQL with Python (CBSE syllabus; not a chapter in the NCERT book)

concepts.text: Need for connectivity: a Python front end working with a MySQL back end
Installing and importing the connector (mysql.connector or pymysql)
Creating a connection with connect(host, user, passwd, database) and checking is_connected()
Creating a cursor object with cursor()
execute() to run SQL statements from Python (CREATE, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT)
commit() to save changes made by INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
Using %s placeholders or format()/f-strings to insert variable values into queries
fetchone() returns the next row as a tuple
fetchall() returns all remaining rows as a list of tuples
fetchmany(n) returns n rows
rowcount attribute gives the number of rows affected or fetched
Closing the cursor and connection
Menu-driven Python program for insert, search, update, delete and display of records in a MySQL table
Exercise types: complete missing statements in connectivity code, write functions to insert/display/update records
